newsitem.title: USA: Whitewater prosecutor says probe will continue.
newsitem.headline: Whitewater prosecutor says probe will continue.

text.p: Whitewater prosecutor Kenneth Starr moved on Wednesday to squelch speculation that his departure means the probe involving President and Mrs. Clinton is over, calling such guesswork wrong and dangerous.
"Those who argue that the investigation is over are wrong," Starr said. "It is wrong, indeed it is dangerous, to draw any conclusions based upon my personal situation."
He added: "The reality is this: This investigation is active and it is at a sensitive stage with ongoing evaluative judgments. Those judgments have not been made."

Starr, the independent counsel who has been investigating business controversies and related cover-up allegations involving President Bill Clinton and Hillary Rodham Clinton since August 1994, issued his caution in a speech to a group of lawyers in a Washington suburb.

The fact he would use a public speaking forum to comment on the status of his politically touchy inquiry -- a highly unusual step -- suggested deep concern over widespread talk that his departure must mean no case has been developed against the Clintons and they can breathe easy.
On Monday, Pepperdine University in Malibu, California, announced in a major surprise that Starr would become dean of its law school in August.
The White House reacted warily to Starr's comments.

"The White House would have no reason to comment. We have no reaon to add to what we said yesterday," said spokesman Mike McCurry, travelling with the president in Boston. He had said on Tuesday that he had "no clue" what Starr's imminent departure might mean, resisting reporters' suggestions it could add up to good news for the Clintons.

Since his appointment in August 1994, Starr has been probing the Clintons' involvement in the Whitewater real estate deal in Arkansas, where he was state governor in the late 1970s and 1980s, and the failure of a savings and loan institution owned by their Whitewater partner, James McDougal.
The inquiry has expanded vastly to cover White House staff activities including whether there were attempts to cover up the Clintons' involvement in matters under investigation.
Despite Starr's disclaimers, news of his departure reportedly sparked glee among White House staffers and led some legal experts to conclude it meant the Clinton investigation had led nowhere.
"There's joy in Mudville," the Washington Post quoted one unidentified official as saying.

"Turn out the lights, the party's over," said Dan Guthrie, attorney for an Arkansas banker indicted by Starr but acquitted on charges he used bank funds to help finance Clinton's political campaigns. "An independent counsel is not going to walk away from a case like this if anything else significant is going to happen."
It was that view that Starr attempted to counter in his speech on Wednesday to the Fairfax County, Virginia, Bar Association in the Washington suburb of McLean.
"I very much wish ... that I could report to the country that the work of the Whitewater investigation is complete," he said. "That is not the case."
Starr, a Republican, praised the team of veteran prosecutors that would carry on that work after he left.

The inquiry is based in Little Rock, Arkansas, as well as in Washington. Besides Whitewater it covers such matters as the 1993 firing of White House travel office employees, the collection of sensitive FBI files by White House employees and the temporary disappearance of subpoenaed evidence involving Hillary Clinton's work as a Little Rock lawyer.
After his speech, Starr talked with reporters and denied an Arkansas newspaper report that he had conducted mock trials of the Clintons to test his case and the jury acquitted them.
"The report is unfounded and untrue," he said.
